description:
Himarë sits at the southern end of the Albanian Riviera, where the mountains of the Ceraunian range drop sharply into the Ionian Sea. The modern town occupies a small coastal plain; above it, on the steep limestone Barbaka hill, stands the old castle-town — Kalaja e Himarës — whose visible remains span 2,600 years of continuous occupation.

The site was first fortified by the ancient Chaonian Greeks, one of the Epirote tribal peoples of the western Balkans, in approximately the 6th century BCE. This places Himara among the oldest documented fortified settlements on the eastern Adriatic-Ionian coast, predating the Roman conquest of Illyria, the Byzantine administration that followed, the medieval Byzantine period, and the Ottoman conquest of Albania in the 15th century — all of which left physical traces in the walls and buildings still visible on the hilltop. The circuit walls incorporate construction from at least three distinct periods, recognisable in the different stone-cutting techniques and mortar compositions as you move around the perimeter.

What distinguishes Himara from most Albanian medieval fortresses is that it has never been fully abandoned. While sites like Gjirokastra and Krujë have substantial castle structures that function as archaeological monuments with depopulated interiors, Himara's old town within the walls has been continuously inhabited; a small resident community maintains stone houses alongside the castle's churches and defensive remains. Walking through the interior is less like visiting an archaeological site than like entering a very old village that happens to be enclosed by medieval walls on a hilltop above the sea.

The views are the other thing. Himara Castle's position on Barbaka hill gives a 360-degree panorama that takes in the full arc of the Albanian Riviera coast from north to south — the beach strips below, the turquoise water of Himarë Bay, and the open Ionian Sea stretching southwest to Corfu, visible as a clear landmass on calm days. This coastal panorama, combined with the mountain backdrop of the Ceraunian range to the east, gives one of the most compositionally striking views in the entire eastern Mediterranean.

The GYG guided tour (t1320024, from €20/person, 4.9★ / 8 reviews) covers the castle and old town over 2 hours, with reserved entry tickets included — two independent GYG signals confirm this: the Includes list names 'Reserved entry tickets' directly, and 'Skip the ticket line' appears as a separate feature tag on the product. The 2-hour format is enough to cover the main structures, the principal viewpoints, and the key interior monuments.
history: The Himara hilltop has been occupied since approximately the 6th century BCE by the ancient Chaonian Greeks of Epirus. The site developed through the Hellenistic period and was incorporated into the Roman Province of Epirus; the lower town by the coast grew during this period while the hilltop retained its fortified character. Byzantine administration maintained and rebuilt the walls over several centuries; the Byzantine period left the most substantial surviving wall sections. Ottoman forces captured Himara in 1479, the same year as much of the Albanian coast; the hilltop remained inhabited through the Ottoman period and into the 20th century. Albania's communist period (1944–1990) placed the largely Greek-speaking Himarë community under particular pressure; the region's Greek population was subject to restrictions on language use and movement. Himara became a site of ethnic and cultural significance in the post-communist period. The castle-town has been partially restored and opened to tourism in the 21st century.
how_to_visit:
**Getting there:** Himara is on the Albanian Riviera, approximately 90 km south of Vlorë and 60 km north of Sarandë. The town is served by buses from Vlorë, Sarandë, and (indirectly) Tirana; the journey from Sarandë takes approximately 1.5 hours. The castle hilltop is reached by a steep footpath from the modern town centre — the ascent takes approximately 20–30 minutes on foot. The GYG guided tour (t1320024) handles the logistical details and includes reserved entry.

**Tickets:** Walk-up entry to the castle grounds is approximately €5 per adult (confirm locally). The GYG guided tour (t1320024, from €20/person, 4.9★ / 8 reviews, 2 hours) includes reserved entry tickets — confirmed by two independent GYG signals — and covers the castle structures, viewpoints, and old-town monuments with a guide. Advance booking is recommended as the tour's small-group capacity fills quickly.

**Practical tips:** The ascent to the castle from the modern town takes 20–30 minutes on a steep path — comfortable shoes with grip are essential, and the path is slippery after rain. Morning visits avoid the midday heat (Albania's summer temperatures regularly reach 35–40°C on the Riviera) and give the best light for photography looking west over the sea. The views to Corfu are clearest in the early morning before heat haze builds. Allow time after the tour to walk the town walls at your own pace.

**Combine with:** [Porto Palermo Castle](/castles/albania/porto-palermo-castle) (~30 km north along the Riviera coast — the Ottoman-era triangular island fortress at the entrance to Porto Palermo bay, one of Albania's most dramatically positioned military sites, accessible by water taxi or a short drive; do not confuse with the Sicilian Porto Palermo) and [Lekuresi Castle](/castles/albania/lekuresi-castle) (~45 km south above Sarandë — the 16th-century Ottoman hilltop fortress with panoramic views over Sarandë bay and Corfu, a natural complement to Himara for an Albanian Riviera hilltop-castles loop).

faqs.question: How old is Himara Castle and what is its architectural history?
faqs.answer: The Himara hilltop has been continuously occupied for approximately 2,600 years — since roughly the 6th century BCE, when it was a settlement of the ancient Chaonian Greeks. The visible remains reflect multiple successive periods: the oldest sections of the circuit walls date to the Byzantine period (roughly 6th–13th century CE), with earlier foundations below that have been archaeologically investigated but are not always visible to casual visitors. Ottoman construction and rebuilding after the 15th-century conquest are also visible in the wall fabric. The interior old town's stone houses range from Ottoman-era through 19th and early 20th century construction. The result is a site where different historical periods are layered rather than a single coherent medieval fortress: walking the walls involves moving through construction from three or four distinct civilisations.

faqs.question: Is Himara safe to visit and how developed is the tourist infrastructure?
faqs.answer: Himara is safe for tourists and has developed considerably since Albania opened to mass tourism in the 2010s. The modern town has hotels, restaurants, and beach facilities serving the Albanian Riviera tourist season; the castle is an established tourist site with a basic ticket booth and maintained access path. The main practical considerations are the steep approach to the castle (not suitable for limited-mobility visitors) and summer heat (July–August temperatures on the Riviera regularly reach 35–40°C; morning visits are strongly recommended). The Albanian Riviera more broadly has become one of the Mediterranean's most-discussed emerging destinations, so infrastructure in the coastal towns is improving rapidly; Himara's road access has improved significantly with highway works connecting it to Sarandë and Vlorë.

faqs.question: Can I see Corfu from Himara Castle?
faqs.answer: Yes — on clear days, Corfu (Kerkyra) is visible as a clear landmass from the Himara Castle viewpoints, approximately 35–40 km to the southwest across the Ionian Sea. The visibility depends on conditions: early mornings before heat haze builds are the most reliable for clear views; afternoon haze in summer can partially obscure the island. The Corfu Channel visible from Himara was historically one of the most contested maritime passages in the eastern Mediterranean, and the sight of Corfu from the castle gives immediate physical context to why the Albanian Riviera coast was strategically important across its long history. The 2-hour guided tour (t1320024) covers the principal viewpoints and the guide can explain what is visible and its historical significance.
